reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and standard clinical genetics texts
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in the untranslated RMRP gene, encoding the RNA component of the ribonuclease MRP complex
Produces a metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with disproportionate short-limbed short stature and characteristically fine, sparse, light and brittle hair
Skeletal features include bowed legs, limited elbow extension, ligamentous laxity and a normal-sized skull with metaphyseal changes on radiographs
A variable combined immunodeficiency affects cellular immunity in particular, causing susceptibility to severe viral infections such as varicella
Hirschsprung disease, anaemia and impaired erythropoiesis are recognised associations
There is an increased risk of malignancy, notably lymphoma, other lymphoproliferative disease and skin cancers
It is more prevalent in the Amish and Finnish populations owing to founder variants
Diagnosis combines the skeletal and hair phenotype with immunological evaluation and molecular testing of RMRP
reference.pathophysiology: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia is caused by biallelic variants in RMRP, which encodes the non-coding RNA subunit of the RNase MRP endoribonuclease. This complex participates in ribosomal RNA processing, cell-cycle-related messenger RNA cleavage and mitochondrial RNA processing. Impaired function disturbs chondrocyte proliferation (metaphyseal dysplasia and short stature), hair follicle growth, lymphocyte proliferation (immunodeficiency) and erythropoiesis, and contributes to the increased predisposition to malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Other metaphyseal chondrodysplasias such as the Schmid type
Achondroplasia and other short-limbed skeletal dysplasias
Adenosine deaminase deficiency with skeletal changes
Cartilage-hair hypoplasia-anauxetic dysplasia spectrum severe variants
additionalInvestigations: Lymphocyte subsets and proliferation studies and immunoglobulin levels
Full blood count to detect anaemia and cytopenias
Evaluation for Hirschsprung disease when bowel symptoms are present
Age-appropriate malignancy surveillance with a low threshold to investigate lymphadenopathy
redFlags: Severe or disseminated viral infection such as varicella in an immunodeficient child
Persistent lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms suggesting lymphoma
Signs of bowel obstruction from associated Hirschsprung disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends largely on the severity of the immunodeficiency and the lifelong increased risk of malignancy; those with severe combined immune impairment have a poorer outlook and may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, whereas milder cases can have near-normal survival with surveillance and infection prevention.
pitfalls: Regarding it as a purely skeletal dysplasia and missing the immunodeficiency
Administering live vaccines before immune status is assessed
Underestimating the risk of severe varicella and other viral infections
Neglecting long-term malignancy surveillance, particularly for lymphoma
management: Management of the immunodeficiency with antimicrobial prophylaxis and immunoglobulin replacement, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe combined immune impairment
Avoidance of live vaccines and heightened vigilance for severe viral infection such as varicella, with prompt antiviral treatment
Lifelong malignancy surveillance, with a low threshold to investigate lymphadenopathy for lymphoma
Monitoring for and management of anaemia and other cytopenias, with transfusion or haematological support as needed
Surgical management of associated Hirschsprung disease where present
Orthopaedic monitoring of the metaphyseal chondrodysplasia and short stature, with growth assessment
Multidisciplinary care across immunology, haematology, clinical genetics and orthopaedics
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with RMRP testing and family screening
